options.a: Ordinary income rates, the same brackets that apply to wages
options.b: Preferential capital gains rates (0%/15%/20% tiers)
options.c: The 28% collectibles rate that applies to all long-term gains
options.d: Ordinary rates plus the 3.8% NIIT for every taxpayer

distractorExplanations.a: Qualified dividends and LTCG get preferential rates; ordinary brackets apply to nonqualified dividends and short-term gains.
distractorExplanations.c: 28% is the maximum rate for collectibles and unrecaptured-type special gains, not the general rate for qualified dividends and LTCG.
distractorExplanations.d: NIIT is a surtax that applies above MAGI thresholds; it does not convert qualified dividends to ordinary-rate income.

options.a: Is claimed instead of itemizing Schedule A deductions
options.b: Is claimed in addition to itemized Schedule A deductions
options.c: Is the same as the personal exemption suspended by TCJA
options.d: Is available to a spouse filing MFS when the other itemizes

distractorExplanations.b: Taxpayers choose the greater of the two; the standard deduction cannot be stacked on top of itemized deductions.
distractorExplanations.c: The personal exemption was a separate per-person amount reduced to $0 by TCJA; the standard deduction is a different allowance.
distractorExplanations.d: If one MFS spouse itemizes, the other spouse's standard deduction is zero, so that spouse must itemize as well.

options.a: Marital status on the first day of the tax year (January 1)
options.b: Marital status and household situation as of year-end
options.c: The status shown on the prior year's return unless changed
options.d: The W-4 withholding status chosen at work

distractorExplanations.a: Marital status is determined on the last day of the tax year (December 31), not on January 1.
distractorExplanations.c: Filing status is redetermined each year from current facts; the prior-year status does not carry over by default.
distractorExplanations.d: The Form W-4 status only sets payroll withholding; it does not determine the filing status on Form 1040.

options.a: Home mortgage interest on a primary residence
options.b: Deductible IRA contribution or student loan interest
options.c: State and local income taxes paid, up to the SALT cap
options.d: Medical expenses exceeding 7.5% of AGI

distractorExplanations.a: Mortgage interest is an itemized deduction on Schedule A, so it is taken after AGI rather than reducing it.
distractorExplanations.c: SALT is an itemized deduction on Schedule A subject to the cap, not an adjustment to income above the line.
distractorExplanations.d: Medical expenses above the 7.5%-of-AGI floor are itemized; they cannot be an adjustment used to compute AGI itself.

options.a: Qualifying children meeting age/relationship/support/residency tests
options.b: Any dependent of any age, including qualifying relatives
options.c: Children under 19, or under 24 if full-time students
options.d: Dependent care costs for children under 13 while both parents work or look for work

distractorExplanations.b: Dependents who are not qualifying children under 17 get the $500 credit for other dependents, not the Child Tax Credit.
distractorExplanations.c: Under-19/under-24-student is the dependency age test; the Child Tax Credit requires the child to be under 17 at year-end.
distractorExplanations.d: Care costs for children under 13 belong to the Child and Dependent Care Credit on Form 2441, a separate credit.

options.a: Federal income tax withheld from a sole proprietor's draws
options.b: Social Security and Medicare taxes on net earnings from self-employment
options.c: Social Security tax only, with Medicare covered by Part B premiums later
options.d: FUTA unemployment tax on the owner's own business profits

distractorExplanations.a: SE tax is not income tax, and owner draws are not wages, so nothing is withheld from them for income tax.
distractorExplanations.c: SE tax includes both the 12.4% Social Security and 2.9% Medicare portions; Part B premiums are a separate cost.
distractorExplanations.d: FUTA is an employer tax on employee wages; sole proprietors do not pay FUTA on their own net earnings.

options.a: Fair market value at year-end, marked to market annually
options.b: Cost (including commissions) adjusted for certain events
options.c: Cost excluding commissions, which are deducted separately
options.d: The company's book value per share on the purchase date

distractorExplanations.a: Mark-to-market applies to §475 traders who elect it; ordinary investors keep a cost basis in purchased stock.
distractorExplanations.c: Purchase commissions are added to basis; they are not a separate deduction, especially with miscellaneous deductions suspended.
distractorExplanations.d: Book value per share is a corporate accounting figure; an investor's basis is what the investor actually paid.

options.a: Offset gains plus $3,000 of ordinary income, then carry back three years
options.b: Offset capital gains and then up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year
options.c: Offset capital gains and then up to $5,000 of ordinary income per year
options.d: Offset only long-term gains if the loss was long-term

distractorExplanations.a: Individual capital losses carry forward indefinitely; the 3-year carryback applies to C corporation capital losses.
distractorExplanations.c: The annual ordinary-income offset is $3,000 ($1,500 MFS), not $5,000; the excess carries forward.
distractorExplanations.d: After netting within each holding-period group, a net long-term loss can offset net short-term gain and vice versa.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-individua.explanation: Net capital loss deduction against ordinary income is limited annually; excess carries forward. Net losses offset gains first, then up to $3,000 ($1,500 MFS) of ordinary income per year, with the excess carried forward.

options.a: A child's unearned income above thresholds, taxed at parents' rates
options.b: A child's earned wages above the standard deduction, taxed at parents' rates
options.c: Unearned income of any dependent, including adults over age 24
options.d: Gifts a child receives from parents above the annual exclusion

distractorExplanations.b: Kiddie tax applies to unearned income such as interest, dividends, and gains; a child's wages are taxed at the child's own rates.
distractorExplanations.c: Kiddie tax covers children under 18, or under 19/under 24 if full-time students with limited earned income, not older dependents.
distractorExplanations.d: Gifts are not income to the child; amounts above the annual exclusion are a gift tax reporting issue for the donor.

options.a: As an above-the-line educator expense deduction up to the annual limit
options.b: As an itemized deduction subject to the 2%-of-AGI floor
options.c: As an above-the-line deduction with no annual dollar limit
options.d: As a nonrefundable education credit on Form 8863 for classroom supplies

distractorExplanations.b: The 2%-floor miscellaneous itemized deduction is suspended; eligible educators use the separate above-the-line deduction.
distractorExplanations.c: The educator expense deduction is capped at $300 per eligible educator ($600 if both spouses qualify).
distractorExplanations.d: Form 8863 is for the AOTC and Lifetime Learning Credit; classroom supplies use the educator expense adjustment.

options.a: Provisional income / combined income thresholds
options.b: The taxpayer's age when benefits were first claimed
options.c: Adjusted gross income alone, excluding tax-exempt interest
options.d: Earned income above the annual earnings-test limit

distractorExplanations.b: Claiming age changes the benefit amount, but the taxable portion depends on combined income versus the base amounts.
distractorExplanations.c: Combined income adds half of benefits and tax-exempt interest to other income; AGI by itself is not the test.
distractorExplanations.d: The SSA earnings test can withhold benefits before full retirement age; it does not set the taxable percentage.

options.a: Long-term capital gains rates plus a 10% additional tax
options.b: Ordinary income tax plus 10% additional tax unless an exception applies
options.c: Ordinary income tax plus a 25% additional tax unless an exception applies
options.d: A 20% additional tax but no income tax if rolled within 90 days

distractorExplanations.a: Traditional IRA distributions are ordinary income; capital gains rates do not apply to IRA payouts.
distractorExplanations.c: 25% is the SIMPLE IRA rate in the first two years of participation; the general early-distribution tax is 10%.
distractorExplanations.d: Rollovers must be completed within 60 days, and a completed rollover avoids both income tax and the 10% additional tax.

options.a: Qualified education expenses for the first four years of postsecondary education
options.b: Qualified expenses for graduate or professional degree courses
options.c: Qualified education expenses for any year of postsecondary study, without a year limit
options.d: Tuition for K-12 private schools paid from a 529 plan

distractorExplanations.b: Graduate courses fall under the Lifetime Learning Credit; the AOTC covers the first four years of undergraduate study.
distractorExplanations.c: The AOTC can be claimed for no more than four tax years per student; it is the Lifetime Learning Credit that has no year limit.
distractorExplanations.d: K-12 tuition can be a qualified 529 distribution but is not an AOTC expense; the AOTC needs postsecondary enrollment.

options.a: In one payment with the return by the April filing deadline
options.b: In quarterly installments (Apr/Jun/Sep/Jan dates)
options.c: In equal quarterly installments in Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec
options.d: Monthly by the 15th, matching the payroll deposit schedule

distractorExplanations.a: Paying everything with the return can trigger the underpayment penalty; estimates are due in four installments.
distractorExplanations.c: Those are calendar-quarter ends; individual estimates are due April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.
distractorExplanations.d: Monthly deposit schedules apply to employment taxes withheld by employers, not to individual estimated tax.

options.a: Form 1120-S and issues Schedule K-1s to partners
options.b: Form 1065 and issues Schedule K-1s to partners
options.c: Form 1041 and issues Schedule K-1s to beneficiaries
options.d: Form 1099-NEC to each partner for their share

distractorExplanations.a: Form 1120-S is the S corporation return; partnerships file Form 1065, though both entity types issue K-1s.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 1041 is the estate and trust income tax return; its K-1s go to beneficiaries, not to partners.
distractorExplanations.d: Partners receive Schedule K-1, not Form 1099-NEC; a partner is not a nonemployee contractor of the partnership.

options.a: Is taxed at the flat 21% corporate rate
options.b: Passes through to shareholders
options.c: Is taxed twice, at entity and shareholder levels
options.d: Is subject to SE tax for each shareholder

distractorExplanations.a: The flat 21% rate applies to C corporations; S corporations generally pay no entity-level income tax.
distractorExplanations.c: Double taxation is the C corporation model; S corporation income is taxed once, at the shareholder level.
distractorExplanations.d: S corporation pass-through income is not self-employment income; shareholder wages bear FICA instead.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-businesse.explanation: S corps are pass-throughs; reasonable compensation rules matter for shareholder-employees. Basis, AAA, and reasonable-compensation rules for shareholder-employee wages still apply.

options.a: Form 1120 and pays entity-level tax
options.b: Form 1120-S and pays entity-level tax
options.c: Form 1065 and passes income to owners
options.d: Form 1120-H and pays a flat 30% rate

distractorExplanations.b: Form 1120-S is for S corporations, which generally pass income through rather than paying entity-level tax.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 1065 is the partnership return; C corporations file Form 1120 and pay tax at the entity level.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 1120-H is the homeowners association election return; ordinary C corporations file Form 1120 at 21%.

options.a: Allows SSTB owners the full 20% deduction at any income level
options.b: May allow up to 20% deduction of QBI for eligible pass-throughs
options.c: Allows C corporations a 20% deduction against the 21% rate
options.d: Is a 20% credit against self-employment tax for sole proprietors

distractorExplanations.a: Above the taxable-income threshold, an SSTB owner's deduction phases out and is eliminated at the top of the range.
distractorExplanations.c: §199A is for individuals, trusts, and estates with pass-through income; C corporations cannot claim it.
distractorExplanations.d: The QBI deduction reduces taxable income; it does not reduce self-employment tax and is not a credit.

options.a: Schedule C (Form 1040)
options.b: Schedule E (Form 1040)
options.c: Schedule SE (Form 1040)
options.d: Form 1065 with one partner

distractorExplanations.b: Schedule E reports rents, royalties, and pass-through K-1 income, not an active sole proprietorship's profit.
distractorExplanations.c: Schedule SE computes self-employment tax on the profit; the profit itself is figured on Schedule C.
distractorExplanations.d: A partnership requires at least two owners; a one-owner unincorporated business reports on Schedule C.

options.a: 100% deductible when provided by a restaurant
options.b: Subject to 50% limitation in many cases
options.c: Subject to an 80% limitation for most taxpayers
options.d: Fully nondeductible, like entertainment

distractorExplanations.a: The temporary 100% restaurant-meal deduction expired after 2022; business meals are back to the 50% limit.
distractorExplanations.c: 80% applies to DOT hours-of-service workers; the general business-meal limit is 50%.
distractorExplanations.d: TCJA disallowed entertainment, but business meals with a business purpose remain 50% deductible.

options.a: A disregarded entity taxed as a sole proprietorship
options.b: A C corporation unless it files Form 2553 for S status
options.c: A partnership filing Form 1065 with one K-1
options.d: An S corporation by default for federal tax

distractorExplanations.b: Corporate status is not the default for a single-member LLC; it requires an election on Form 8832 or 2553.
distractorExplanations.c: Default partnership classification requires two or more members; a single-member LLC is disregarded.
distractorExplanations.d: S status requires a timely Form 2553 election; it is not the default classification for any LLC.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-businesse.explanation: Single-member LLCs are disregarded by default; Form 8832/2553 elections can change classification. A Form 8832 or 2553 election can change this default classification.

options.a: Required quarterly when each Form 941 is filed, for every employer
options.b: Required on IRS schedules (monthly/semiweekly, etc.) based on lookback
options.c: Required monthly or semiweekly based on the current quarter's payroll amounts
options.d: Due annually with Form 940 along with the FUTA return

distractorExplanations.a: Paying with Form 941 is allowed for small quarterly liabilities under $2,500; most employers deposit monthly or semiweekly.
distractorExplanations.c: The deposit schedule is set by the lookback period (12 months ending the prior June 30), not current-quarter payroll.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 940 reports FUTA; withheld income tax and FICA are deposited on the monthly or semiweekly schedule.

options.a: 60% of AGI, the same limit as for individuals
options.b: A percentage of taxable income (commonly 10%)
options.c: A percentage of gross receipts (commonly 25%)
options.d: A percentage of book income (commonly 5%)

distractorExplanations.a: 60% of AGI is the individual cash-to-public-charity limit; corporations use a taxable-income percentage.
distractorExplanations.c: The corporate limit is based on taxable income, not gross receipts; 25% applies to certain food-inventory gifts.
distractorExplanations.d: The limit is computed on taxable income with adjustments, not book income, and the general ceiling is 10%.

options.a: Businesses with inventory
options.b: Service firms with no inventory
options.c: Landlords renting residential units
options.d: Employees with unreimbursed costs

distractorExplanations.b: Service businesses without merchandise generally have no COGS; their costs are ordinary operating expenses.
distractorExplanations.c: Rental property costs are depreciation and operating expenses on Schedule E, not cost of goods sold.
distractorExplanations.d: Employees have no COGS; unreimbursed employee expenses are suspended miscellaneous itemized deductions.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-businesse.explanation: Inventory businesses compute COGS under accounting/tax inventory methods. Gross receipts minus COGS equals gross profit.

options.a: Wages are subject to employment taxes while distributions generally are not
options.b: Distributions are subject to SE tax unless wages are paid first
options.c: Wages reduce the shareholder's stock basis while distributions do not
options.d: Wages paid to shareholders are not deductible by the corporation

distractorExplanations.b: S corporation distributions are not subject to SE tax; the risk is recharacterization of distributions as wages.
distractorExplanations.c: Distributions reduce stock basis; wages are a deductible corporate expense and do not reduce shareholder basis.
distractorExplanations.d: Reasonable wages are deductible by the S corporation; the scrutiny concerns avoided FICA on disguised wages.

options.a: Deductible up to $50,000 in year one, with the rest amortized over 180 months
options.b: Subject to capitalization with limited immediate expensing and amortization rules
options.c: Capitalized and recovered over 39 years like nonresidential real property
options.d: Nondeductible until the business is sold, then added to the basis

distractorExplanations.a: $50,000 is the phase-out threshold; the immediate deduction is up to $5,000 each for start-up and organizational costs.
distractorExplanations.c: Start-up and organizational costs are amortized over 180 months (15 years), not the 39-year building life.
distractorExplanations.d: Under §195 and §248 these costs are partly expensed and amortized; they are not frozen until a sale.

options.a: A state license issued after passing the Uniform CPA Exam
options.b: IRS enrollment (Special Enrollment Exam or qualifying IRS experience)
options.c: Completing the Annual Filing Season Program and receiving a Record of Completion
options.d: Obtaining a PTIN and passing an IRS suitability check

distractorExplanations.a: Passing the CPA exam leads to a state CPA license; EAs are enrolled federally by the IRS, not licensed by states.
distractorExplanations.c: AFSP gives limited representation rights to unenrolled preparers; it does not make someone an Enrolled Agent.
distractorExplanations.d: A PTIN is needed to prepare returns for pay but grants no representation rights; EAs pass the SEE or qualify by experience.

options.a: Authorize a third party to inspect tax information without representing
options.b: Appoint a power of attorney to represent a taxpayer before the IRS
options.c: Allow a designee to receive the taxpayer's refund check
options.d: Designate a third party to discuss only the current return

distractorExplanations.a: Information-only authorization is Form 8821; Form 2848 grants representation rights for listed matters.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 2848 cannot authorize endorsing or cashing refund checks; refund direction is handled on the return or Form 8888.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the third-party designee checkbox on Form 1040; Form 2848 appoints a representative for listed matters and periods.

options.a: Power of attorney allowing the appointee to represent the taxpayer
options.b: Tax information authorization without full representation powers
options.c: Third-party designee authority that lapses one year after the due date
options.d: Authorization for a preparer to e-file the return using Form 8879

distractorExplanations.a: Representation requires Form 2848; Form 8821 lets the designee receive and inspect information but not advocate.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes the Form 1040 third-party designee checkbox, which expires a year after the return due date.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 8879 is the IRS e-file signature authorization; Form 8821 is a tax information authorization.

options.a: Provide every record requested, including privileged material, without any prior review
options.b: Respond timely, provide relevant records, and advocate within Circular 230 ethics
options.c: Refuse all IDRs until the IRS issues a formal summons
options.d: Let the client meet the agent alone to show good faith cooperation

distractorExplanations.a: Representatives may assert privileges and limit responses to relevant records; turning everything over unreviewed is poor practice.
distractorExplanations.c: Refusing IDRs escalates the case and invites a summons; prompt cooperation within proper scope is expected.
distractorExplanations.d: With a valid Form 2848 the representative can handle the meeting; the client generally need not attend alone.

options.a: Form 12153 (within the stated deadline after NFTL/levy notice)
options.b: Form 9423 (Collection Appeals Program request after a levy notice)
options.c: Form 911 (Taxpayer Advocate assistance request after a levy notice)
options.d: Form 843 (claim for refund and abatement after an NFTL filing)

distractorExplanations.b: Form 9423 requests a CAP appeal, a faster process without Tax Court review; CDP hearings use Form 12153.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 911 requests Taxpayer Advocate help; it does not preserve the statutory CDP hearing right.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 843 claims refunds or penalty abatement; it is not a request for a collection due process hearing.

options.a: Pay the full debt in monthly installments over six years
options.b: Settle a tax debt for less than the full amount
options.c: Remove penalties for a first-time noncompliant year
options.d: Pause collection while the taxpayer cannot pay expenses

distractorExplanations.a: Paying in full over time is an installment agreement; an OIC settles for less than the full amount owed.
distractorExplanations.c: Penalty removal for a clean history is First-Time Abatement, a separate administrative waiver, not an OIC.
distractorExplanations.d: Pausing collection for hardship is Currently Not Collectible status; the debt itself is not reduced.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-represent.explanation: OIC is a collection alternative under specific IRS standards. Grounds are doubt as to collectibility, doubt as to liability, or effective tax administration.

options.a: Petition the U.S. Tax Court within 90 days (150 if addressed outside the U.S.)
options.b: Request a CDP hearing within 30 days to contest the deficiency
options.c: Petition the U.S. Tax Court within 30 days (60 days if addressed outside the U.S.)
options.d: File suit in district court within 90 days without paying the tax

distractorExplanations.b: CDP hearings follow lien or levy notices; the deficiency notice opens the 90-day Tax Court window instead.
distractorExplanations.c: The SNOD petition period is 90 days (150 if addressed outside the U.S.), not 30 or 60 days.
distractorExplanations.d: District court refund suits generally require full payment first; prepayment review is available in Tax Court.

options.a: It is revoked, withdrawn, superseded, or the matter/period concludes as specified
options.b: The taxpayer hires a different preparer to file the following year's income tax return
options.c: Six years pass from the date the Form 2848 was signed
options.d: A new Form 2848 is filed for a different tax form and period

distractorExplanations.b: A new preparer does not revoke a Form 2848; revocation requires written notice or a new POA that does not retain the old one.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 2848 has no fixed six-year life; it ends by revocation, withdrawal, superseding, or as listed matters end.
distractorExplanations.d: A new POA supersedes earlier ones for the same matters; a different form or period leaves the prior POA in place.

options.a: IRS-recognized representatives on authorizations
options.b: Paid preparers on the returns they sign for clients
options.c: Businesses on payroll returns and deposits
options.d: E-file providers transmitting returns

distractorExplanations.b: Preparers are identified on returns by PTIN; CAF numbers track representatives on Forms 2848 and 8821.
distractorExplanations.c: Businesses use EINs on payroll returns and deposits; the CAF number is issued to authorized representatives.
distractorExplanations.d: E-file providers are identified by EFIN; the CAF number relates to POA and tax information authorizations.

options.a: Re-examine the return and develop new issues for assessment
options.b: Resolve disputes fairly considering hazards of litigation
options.c: Decide the case strictly on the law with no settlement authority
options.d: Issue a statutory notice of deficiency at the first meeting

distractorExplanations.a: Appeals does not raise new issues or reopen issues the examiner conceded; it settles existing disputes.
distractorExplanations.c: Appeals has settlement authority and weighs litigation hazards; it is not a court ruling strictly on the law.
distractorExplanations.d: Appeals may issue an SNOD if no settlement is reached, but its goal is settlement, not immediate assessment.

options.a: Requires the taxpayer to attend in person with the representative
options.b: May proceed with the authorized representative present
options.c: Must be rescheduled until the taxpayer signs a new Form 8821
options.d: Is limited to written questions once a Form 2848 is on file

distractorExplanations.a: Generally the taxpayer need not attend when a representative is authorized, unless the taxpayer is summoned.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 8821 grants information access without advocacy; representation in interviews comes from Form 2848.
distractorExplanations.d: A Form 2848 does not restrict interviews to written questions; the representative may attend and speak.

options.a: Meeting IRS criteria (compliance history, specific penalties)
options.b: Showing reasonable cause such as illness or a natural disaster
options.c: A clean compliance history for the prior five years
options.d: Owing less than $10,000 in total tax for the year

distractorExplanations.b: Reasonable cause is a separate relief basis; FTA is granted on a clean three-year history without proving cause.
distractorExplanations.c: FTA looks back three years, not five, for no prior significant penalties.
distractorExplanations.d: FTA has no dollar ceiling; eligibility turns on compliance history, filing, and payment arrangements.

options.a: Finally determine tax liability for specific matters
options.b: Extend the assessment statute of limitations for open years
options.c: Waive restrictions on assessment while preserving appeal rights
options.d: Record a taxpayer's acceptance of an installment plan

distractorExplanations.b: Extending the assessment statute uses Form 872; closing agreements on Forms 866/906 finally settle liabilities.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes Form 870, which consents to assessment but is not a binding final closing agreement.
distractorExplanations.d: Installment agreements use Form 9465 or 433-D; closing agreements finally determine tax liability.

options.a: Practice before the U.S. Tax Court by attorneys and nonattorney practitioners
options.b: Practice before the IRS by attorneys, CPAs, EAs, and others eligible to practice
options.c: State tax practice by CPAs and attorneys under each state's board rules
options.d: Treasury employees' ethics when communicating with tax practitioners

distractorExplanations.a: Tax Court admission is governed by the court's own rules; Circular 230 governs practice before the IRS.
distractorExplanations.c: State boards and bars regulate state licensure; Circular 230 is a federal Treasury regulation for IRS practice.
distractorExplanations.d: Circular 230 regulates practitioners, not IRS employees, whose conduct falls under federal employee ethics rules.

options.a: Anyone who prepares or assists in preparing all or substantially all of a federal tax return for compensation
options.b: Only credentialed preparers (EAs, CPAs, attorneys) who sign returns, not unenrolled seasonal preparers
options.c: Anyone who prepares federal returns, including volunteers at VITA sites and family members who are not paid for it
options.d: Anyone who prepares state returns for compensation, while federal-only preparers use their EFIN instead

distractorExplanations.b: Every paid preparer, credentialed or not, must have a PTIN; unenrolled preparers need one too.
distractorExplanations.c: PTINs are required for compensated preparers; unpaid VITA volunteers and family helpers do not need one.
distractorExplanations.d: The PTIN is a federal requirement for paid federal return preparers; an EFIN identifies an e-file provider, not a preparer.

options.a: Advise the client promptly of the omission and its consequences
options.b: File an amended return for the client once the omission is confirmed
options.c: Report the omission to the IRS if the client declines to correct it
options.d: Withdraw from the engagement before discussing the omission

distractorExplanations.b: §10.21 requires advising the client; the practitioner cannot amend without the client's authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: Circular 230 does not require reporting a client's omission to the IRS; the duty is to advise the client.
distractorExplanations.d: Withdrawal may be considered later, but §10.21 first requires promptly advising the client of the omission.

options.a: Completing Form 8867 and applying knowledge/inquiry standards
options.b: Obtaining Form 8879 and keeping the client's signed engagement letter
options.c: Completing Form 8862 for every client claiming the credits
options.d: Retaining the completed checklist for two years from filing

distractorExplanations.b: Form 8879 is the e-file signature authorization; due diligence for these credits requires Form 8867 and inquiry.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 8862 is filed after a prior-year credit disallowance; preparer due diligence uses Form 8867.
distractorExplanations.d: Due diligence records must be kept for three years from the latest relevant filing date, not two.

options.a: Never disclose client tax information except as authorized or legally required
options.b: Disclosing return information to a lender when the client verbally agrees
options.c: Sharing client data with affiliated firms without consent for marketing
options.d: Disclosing client details to other preparers in the firm's online forum

distractorExplanations.b: §7216 consent must be written and signed in the prescribed format; a verbal agreement is not valid consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Using return information for marketing, even with affiliates, requires prior written §7216 consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharing identifiable client details outside a need-to-know purpose breaches confidentiality without consent.

options.a: Be based on reasonable factual/legal assumptions and not be misleading
options.b: Be issued as a covered opinion with a 'more likely than not' level
options.c: Assume the IRS will not audit the return when evaluating the position
options.d: Rely on the client's statements even if the practitioner knows they are false

distractorExplanations.b: The covered-opinion rules of former §10.35 were withdrawn in 2014; §10.37 now sets a reasonableness standard.
distractorExplanations.c: §10.37 forbids taking audit likelihood into account when evaluating a position or giving written advice.
distractorExplanations.d: A practitioner may rely in good faith on client information, but not on representations known to be incorrect.

options.a: Reconstructed records labeled as originals
options.b: Accurate copies/originals as appropriate
options.c: Originals only, since copies are not accepted
options.d: Summaries prepared by the practitioner instead

distractorExplanations.a: Reconstructed records may be submitted if clearly identified as reconstructions; labeling them as originals is false.
distractorExplanations.c: The IRS generally accepts legible copies; sending originals is often unnecessary and risks losing them.
distractorExplanations.d: Summaries can help, but the IRS may require underlying records; summaries do not replace substantiation.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-practices.explanation: Submitting false documents is criminal/ethical violation. Never submit documents known to be false.

options.a: State that the practitioner is enrolled to practice before the IRS
options.b: Claim IRS employee status or guaranteed results deceptively
options.c: Include a fee schedule for return preparation and representation
options.d: Use the term 'enrolled agent' in the firm's name or website

distractorExplanations.a: §10.30 expressly permits an EA to describe the credential as enrolled to practice before the IRS.
distractorExplanations.c: Published fee information is permitted under §10.30 as long as the practitioner honors the stated fees.
distractorExplanations.d: Using 'enrolled agent' truthfully is allowed; the prohibition is on 'certified' or implying IRS employment.

options.a: Oral informed consent from each affected client, documented later if a dispute arises
options.b: Informed consent in writing when representation of conflicting interests is otherwise permitted
options.c: Written notice to the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility before representing both
options.d: Retaining written consent for one year after the representation ends

distractorExplanations.a: §10.29 requires consent confirmed in writing by each affected client within 30 days; oral consent alone fails.
distractorExplanations.c: Conflict waivers come from the affected clients, not OPR; OPR does not pre-approve representation.
distractorExplanations.d: §10.29 requires keeping written consents for at least 36 months from the end of the representation, not one year.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-practices.explanation: Conflicts need waiver/consent meeting Circular 230 conditions or withdrawal. Otherwise the practitioner must decline the representation.

options.a: Strong ID verification, secure systems, and not participating in refund fraud
options.b: Sharing EFINs with trusted seasonal preparers to speed up filing season
options.c: Disabling MFA on tax software so multiple staff can log in quickly
options.d: Accepting photo IDs by email without checking them against the client

distractorExplanations.b: EFINs are issued to a specific provider and may not be shared; sharing them enables refund fraud.
distractorExplanations.c: IRS safeguards guidance requires multi-factor authentication; disabling it weakens protection of client data.
distractorExplanations.d: Emailed IDs must still be verified against the person; unverified IDs are a common stolen-identity fraud path.

options.a: Understatements due to unreasonable positions / willful/reckless conduct
options.b: Any understatement the IRS assesses, even with substantial authority
options.c: Failure to sign the return or include the preparer's PTIN
options.d: Failing to furnish the client a copy of the completed return

distractorExplanations.b: §6694 does not apply to positions supported by substantial authority; an IRS adjustment alone is not enough.
distractorExplanations.c: Missing signatures or PTINs are penalized under §6695, a separate preparer penalty.
distractorExplanations.d: Not furnishing a client copy is a §6695(a) penalty, not the §6694 understatement penalty.

options.a: Practitioners must return client-provided records
options.b: Practitioners may hold the records until fees are paid
options.c: Practitioners must return records and their own workpapers
options.d: Practitioners must return records only to a successor preparer

distractorExplanations.b: §10.28 requires returning client records needed to comply with tax obligations even when fees are disputed.
distractorExplanations.c: Workpapers and the practitioner's own work product may be withheld in a fee dispute when state law allows.
distractorExplanations.d: §10.28 requires returning records to the client on request, not merely to a successor preparer.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-practices.explanation: Circular 230 addresses return of client records; holding originals for unpaid fees is restricted. Practitioners may keep copies; their own work product may be retained subject to fee-dispute rules.

options.a: Take only matters they can handle competently or become competent through study/consultation
options.b: Accept a new matter if a supervisor will sign the return, even without relevant knowledge
options.c: Rely on the client's legal conclusions when the client is a licensed attorney
options.d: Meet competence by completing the minimum continuing education hours each year

distractorExplanations.b: §10.35 requires the practitioner personally have or acquire the knowledge, skill, and preparation needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Practitioners must evaluate legal issues themselves; a client's legal conclusion does not satisfy competence.
distractorExplanations.d: CE is a separate enrollment-renewal requirement; competence is judged matter by matter under §10.35.

options.a: Being unmarried and maintaining a home for a qualifying person for more than half the year
options.b: Being married and living with the spouse while paying all costs of a home for a child
options.c: Being unmarried and maintaining a home for a qualifying person for at least three months of the year
options.d: Being a surviving spouse with a dependent child within two years of the spouse's death

distractorExplanations.b: A married taxpayer can use HOH only if considered unmarried, which requires living apart from the spouse for the last six months.
distractorExplanations.c: The qualifying person must live with the taxpayer for more than half the year, not just three months.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes qualifying surviving spouse status, which is more favorable than HOH and has its own tests.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-individua.explanation: HOH has specific relationship, support, and abode tests beyond simply having a dependent. A taxpayer who is considered unmarried can also qualify.

options.a: Taxable as ordinary income but excluded from state tax
options.b: Taxed at 0%/15%/20% preferential rates like qualified dividends
options.c: Exempt from federal tax but subject to self-employment tax
options.d: Exempt from federal income tax (state tax treatment may differ)

distractorExplanations.a: It is the reverse: qualified muni interest is federally exempt, while states may tax out-of-state bond interest.
distractorExplanations.b: Muni interest is excluded from gross income, not taxed at preferential qualified dividend rates.
distractorExplanations.c: Muni interest is investment income, not self-employment income, so SE tax does not apply to it.

options.a: Modified adjusted gross income exceeds thresholds that depend on filing status
options.b: The taxpayer or spouse is covered by an employer 401(k) plan during the year
options.c: The taxpayer is over age 70½ at the end of the year
options.d: Earned income exceeds the annual Social Security wage base limit

distractorExplanations.b: Workplace plan coverage limits deductibility of traditional IRA contributions, not Roth IRA eligibility.
distractorExplanations.c: Roth contributions have no age limit, and SECURE Act removed the age cap for traditional IRA contributions too.
distractorExplanations.d: Roth eligibility uses MAGI phase-out ranges by filing status, not the Social Security wage base.

options.a: Wages exceed the threshold for the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax
options.b: Modified AGI exceeds statutory thresholds and net investment income is present
options.c: Net investment income exceeds $250,000 for every filing status
options.d: Taxable income exceeds the top of the 35% bracket and gains are present

distractorExplanations.a: The 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies to wages and SE income; NIIT is a 3.8% tax on investment income.
distractorExplanations.c: Thresholds apply to MAGI ($200,000 single, $250,000 MFJ, $125,000 MFS), not to investment income alone.
distractorExplanations.d: NIIT uses fixed MAGI thresholds that are not indexed, not tax bracket breakpoints.

options.a: Replaces regular tax with a flat 21% rate on alternative minimum taxable income
options.b: Applies to anyone with income above the AMT exemption amount, even if regular tax is higher
options.c: Recalculates tax using broader income and limited deductions, then compares to regular tax
options.d: Recalculates tax using the same deductions but a higher 28% flat rate on all income

distractorExplanations.a: Individual AMT rates are 26% and 28%; 21% is the regular C corporation income tax rate.
distractorExplanations.b: AMT is owed when tentative minimum tax exceeds regular tax; income above the exemption alone does not trigger it.
distractorExplanations.d: AMT adds back items like SALT and uses a 26%/28% schedule after an exemption, not one flat rate with the same deductions.

options.a: Tax-deductible contributions and growth, with withdrawals taxed like a traditional IRA
options.b: After-tax contributions, tax-free growth, and tax-free withdrawals for any purpose after 55
options.c: Deductible contributions and tax-free medical withdrawals, but use-it-or-lose-it balances each year
options.d: Tax-deductible/funded contributions, tax-free growth, and tax-free qualified medical withdrawals

distractorExplanations.a: Qualified medical HSA withdrawals are tax-free; nonqualified withdrawals are taxed, plus 20% before age 65.
distractorExplanations.b: HSA contributions are deductible, and nonmedical withdrawals are taxable; age 65 (not 55) removes the 20% penalty.
distractorExplanations.c: Use-it-or-lose-it describes health FSAs; HSA balances roll over and stay with the account owner.

options.a: Form 8962 with the tax return, comparing actual income to Marketplace estimates
options.b: Form 1095-A attached to the return, reconciling actual income to the estimate
options.c: Form 8965 with the tax return, comparing actual coverage to Marketplace estimates
options.d: Form 1095-B issued by the insurer, with any excess repaid directly to the insurer

distractorExplanations.b: Form 1095-A is the Marketplace statement used as input; the reconciliation itself is computed on Form 8962.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 8965 claimed coverage exemptions for the individual mandate and is obsolete; APTC is reconciled on Form 8962.
distractorExplanations.d: Excess APTC is repaid to the IRS through Form 8962 on the return; Form 1095-B just reports minimum coverage.

options.a: Disallows a gain when substantially identical stock or securities are repurchased within 30 days after the sale
options.b: Disallows a loss when substantially identical stock or securities are repurchased within 30 days before or after the sale
options.c: Disallows a loss when substantially identical stock is repurchased within 61 days after the sale, ignoring purchases before
options.d: Disallows a loss permanently when the same stock is repurchased within 30 days, with no basis adjustment

distractorExplanations.a: Wash sale rules apply to losses, not gains, and the window covers 30 days before as well as after the sale.
distractorExplanations.c: The 61-day window is 30 days before, the sale day, and 30 days after, not 61 days after the sale.
distractorExplanations.d: A wash sale loss is deferred, not lost: it is added to the basis of the replacement shares.

options.a: Business vehicles and equipment traded for similar assets
options.b: Any real property, including a personal residence
options.c: Real property held for investment or business use
options.d: Real property in the U.S. exchanged for foreign real property

distractorExplanations.a: TCJA removed personal property, including vehicles and equipment, from §1031 for exchanges after 2017.
distractorExplanations.b: A personal residence is not held for investment or business use, so it cannot be §1031 property.
distractorExplanations.d: U.S. and foreign real property are not like-kind to each other under §1031(h).

options.a: Ownership and use for three of the last five years
options.b: Reinvesting the proceeds in a new home within two years
options.c: Being age 55 or older at the time of the sale
options.d: Ownership and use tests (typically two of five years)

distractorExplanations.a: The §121 tests require two of the five years before the sale, not three.
distractorExplanations.b: Reinvestment was the pre-1997 rollover rule (§1034); §121 has no reinvestment requirement.
distractorExplanations.c: The age-55 one-time exclusion was repealed in 1997; current §121 has no age requirement.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-individua.explanation: Partial exclusions may apply for certain work/health moves; nonqualified use can reduce exclusion for rental periods after 2008. Limits also apply to how often (generally once every two years) and how much ($250,000/$500,000) gain is excluded.

options.a: Offsets taxable income in later years subject to post-TCJA percentage limitations
options.b: Carries back two years first, then forward up to 20 years
options.c: Offsets 100% of taxable income in later years for up to 20 years
options.d: Offsets taxable income in later years, but expires after five years if unused

distractorExplanations.b: That is the pre-2018 rule; post-2020 NOLs generally carry forward indefinitely, with farm losses carried back two years.
distractorExplanations.c: Post-2017 NOLs are limited to 80% of taxable income but carry forward indefinitely, not for 20 years.
distractorExplanations.d: Post-2017 NOLs do not expire; the 5-year period was the temporary CARES Act carryback for 2018–2020 losses.

options.a: The taxpayer materially participates for at least 750 hours
options.b: The taxpayer actively participates and MAGI is below phase-out thresholds
options.c: The taxpayer actively participates and MAGI is below $200,000
options.d: The rental is a vacation home rented fewer than 15 days per year and used personally

distractorExplanations.a: 750 hours is part of the real estate professional test; the $25,000 allowance requires active participation.
distractorExplanations.c: The $25,000 allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of MAGI, not at $200,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Rentals under 15 days are tax-free and not reported; the special allowance is for active rental real estate.

options.a: The payee's foreign status certification to avoid withholding
options.b: The employee's withholding allowances for federal income tax
options.c: The payee's verified identity for an EIN application
options.d: The payee's taxpayer identification number and certification

distractorExplanations.a: Foreign status is certified on Form W-8BEN; Form W-9 is for U.S. persons providing a TIN.
distractorExplanations.b: Employees give withholding information on Form W-4; Form W-9 goes to payees such as contractors.
distractorExplanations.c: EIN applications use Form SS-4; Form W-9 supplies an existing TIN to a payer for information reporting.

options.a: Deduct a large percentage of qualifying property cost in the year placed in service
options.b: Deduct qualifying property cost in the year placed in service up to a taxable income limit
options.c: Deduct a large percentage of real property cost, including buildings, in the first year
options.d: Take a first-year deduction only for new property not previously used by anyone

distractorExplanations.b: The taxable-income limit applies to §179 expensing; bonus depreciation can create or increase a loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Buildings (27.5/39-year property) do not qualify; bonus applies to property with a recovery period of 20 years or less.
distractorExplanations.d: Since TCJA, used property acquired from unrelated parties also qualifies for bonus depreciation.

options.a: Payments of $600 or more for rent and prizes paid by a business
options.b: Payment card and third-party network transactions above the reporting threshold
options.c: Nonemployee compensation of $600 or more paid in the course of a trade or business
options.d: Nonemployee compensation of $5,000 or more paid to a corporation

distractorExplanations.a: Rents, prizes, and awards are reported on Form 1099-MISC; Form 1099-NEC is for nonemployee compensation.
distractorExplanations.b: Card and payment-app transactions are reported by settlement entities on Form 1099-K, not Form 1099-NEC.
distractorExplanations.d: Payments to corporations are generally exempt from 1099-NEC (attorney fees excepted), and $5,000 is not the threshold.

options.a: Replace the owner's SSN on the owner's own Form 1040
options.b: Report employee wages on Form W-2 in place of each employee's Social Security number
options.c: Obtain the electronic filing identification number required to e-file returns
options.d: Identify the business on tax returns, payroll deposits, and information returns

distractorExplanations.a: An EIN identifies the business; the owner still uses an SSN on the individual Form 1040.
distractorExplanations.b: Form W-2 shows the employer's EIN and each employee's SSN; the EIN does not replace employee SSNs.
distractorExplanations.c: An EFIN comes from the IRS e-file provider application; an EIN is the business taxpayer ID.

options.a: Corporations accumulating earnings beyond reasonable business needs to avoid shareholder-level tax
options.b: Personal holding companies earning mostly passive investment income such as dividends and royalties
options.c: S corporations with accumulated E&P from C years and excess passive investment income
options.d: C corporations paying dividends beyond current earnings and profits to their shareholders

distractorExplanations.b: Passive-income companies face the separate personal holding company tax and are excluded from the accumulated earnings tax.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the §1375 tax on S corporations' excess passive income, not the accumulated earnings tax.
distractorExplanations.d: Distributions exceeding E&P are a return of capital; AET penalizes retaining, not distributing, earnings.

options.a: Deductible currently if the sale price equals fair market value as set by an appraisal
options.b: Disallowed currently, with potential offsetting rules when the related party later sells
options.c: Deferred until the related buyer resells, then deducted by the original seller at that time
options.d: Disallowed currently and added to the related buyer's basis

distractorExplanations.a: §267 disallows losses between related parties even when the price equals appraised fair market value.
distractorExplanations.c: The original seller does not get the loss later; the buyer may use it to reduce gain on a later resale.
distractorExplanations.d: The disallowed loss is not added to the buyer's basis; it can be used to offset the buyer's later gain.

options.a: Expense direct and indirect production costs as period costs
options.b: Capitalize all selling and marketing costs into inventory
options.c: Capitalize certain indirect costs into inventory or produced property
options.d: Capitalize indirect costs even if gross receipts are under $31 million

distractorExplanations.a: UNICAP requires capitalizing allocable direct and indirect costs, not expensing them as period costs.
distractorExplanations.b: Selling, advertising, and distribution costs are excluded from UNICAP; it covers production and resale costs.
distractorExplanations.d: Small businesses meeting the §448(c) gross receipts test ($31 million for 2025) are exempt from UNICAP.

options.a: A short-term capital loss when the debt becomes totally worthless
options.b: An ordinary loss using the reserve method for estimated bad debts
options.c: An ordinary loss for unpaid cash-basis fees not yet reported as income
options.d: An ordinary loss when worthlessness or partial charge-off is established

distractorExplanations.a: Short-term capital loss treatment applies to nonbusiness bad debts; business bad debts are ordinary losses.
distractorExplanations.b: The reserve method is not allowed for most taxpayers; business bad debts use the specific charge-off method.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash-method taxpayers cannot deduct uncollected fees not included in income; there is no basis in the receivable.

options.a: Limits NOL deductions to a percentage of taxable income in carryforward years
options.b: Allows a two-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward with no percentage limit
options.c: Limits NOL carryforwards to 80% of taxable income for 20 years before expiration
options.d: Allows a five-year carryback for losses arising in any tax year

distractorExplanations.b: That is pre-TCJA law; post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely and are capped at 80% of taxable income.
distractorExplanations.c: The 80% cap is right, but post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely rather than expiring after 20 years.
distractorExplanations.d: The five-year carryback was a temporary CARES Act rule for 2018–2020 losses, not current law.

options.a: Distributions above basis are subject to SE tax for active owners
options.b: Too-low wages can recharacterize distributions to avoid payroll taxes
options.c: High wages reduce the corporate AAA and trigger built-in gains tax
options.d: Wages must equal at least 60% of S corporation net income

distractorExplanations.a: Distributions above basis are capital gain, not SE income; the concern is distributions recharacterized as wages.
distractorExplanations.c: Wages are deductible and do not trigger §1374 built-in gains tax; AAA is reduced by distributions and losses.
distractorExplanations.d: No fixed 60% rule exists; reasonable compensation is a facts-and-circumstances test of services rendered.

options.a: Capitalized and amortized over 60 months
options.b: Capitalized and depreciated over 39 years
options.c: Capitalized and amortized over 180 months
options.d: Deducted in full up to $50,000 in year one

distractorExplanations.a: Sixty months was the pre-2004 §195 amortization period; current law uses 180 months.
distractorExplanations.b: 39 years is the nonresidential real property life; start-up costs are amortized over 180 months.
distractorExplanations.d: $50,000 is the phase-out threshold; the immediate deduction is $5,000, reduced dollar-for-dollar above it.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-businesse.explanation: Organizational and start-up costs have specific capitalization and §195 amortization rules. Up to $5,000 can be expensed immediately (phased out above $50,000), with the rest amortized.

options.a: Sharing of graduated corporate tax brackets among members of the controlled group
options.b: Consolidated filing of one Form 1120 for brother-sister groups
options.c: Treatment of each member's employees as independent contractors
options.d: Combined employee counts and benefit plan discrimination testing limits

distractorExplanations.a: Graduated corporate brackets ended with the flat 21% rate under TCJA, so bracket sharing no longer matters.
distractorExplanations.b: Consolidated returns are for affiliated parent-subsidiary groups; brother-sister groups cannot file one return.
distractorExplanations.c: Worker classification uses common-law control tests; controlled group status does not convert employees.

options.a: Prices and terms are consistent with arm's-length dealings between unrelated parties
options.b: Prices match the related parties' cost plus a fixed 10% markup
options.c: Prices and terms follow the parent company's internal budget rates approved by its board
options.d: Prices and terms minimize combined worldwide tax for the group

distractorExplanations.b: Cost plus is one possible method, but no fixed 10% markup is required; results must fall in an arm's-length range.
distractorExplanations.c: Internal budget rates are not a §482 standard; pricing must reflect what unrelated parties would agree to.
distractorExplanations.d: Minimizing worldwide tax is not a §482 standard; the IRS may reallocate income that departs from arm's length.

options.a: Adjusted gross income exceeds thresholds and the business has no W-2 employees
options.b: Taxable income exceeds thresholds and the business is a specified service trade or business
options.c: Taxable income is below thresholds and the business pays no W-2 wages
options.d: The business is an S corporation paying its shareholder-employee reasonable compensation

distractorExplanations.a: Limits key off taxable income before the QBI deduction, not AGI; wage limits matter above the threshold.
distractorExplanations.c: Below the threshold the W-2 wage and UBIA limits do not apply, so the full 20% deduction is generally available.
distractorExplanations.d: S corporation income qualifies; the owner's reasonable compensation is excluded from QBI but causes no limitation.

options.a: Sign the original return on the taxpayer's behalf once a Form 2848 is filed
options.b: Answer only the IRS correspondence sent to the representative, leaving taxpayer notices aside
options.c: Bring a second client's records to show the agent consistent industry practice
options.d: Review the power of attorney, understand the scope, and communicate through authorized channels

distractorExplanations.a: A Form 2848 does not authorize signing a return unless the narrow Reg. 1.6012-1(a)(5) conditions are met and stated.
distractorExplanations.b: Notices sent to the taxpayer also need a response; representatives coordinate replies to relevant IRS correspondence.
distractorExplanations.c: Sharing another client's records breaches §7216 and Circular 230 confidentiality duties.

options.a: 90 days from the date the notice was mailed
options.b: 120 days from the date the notice was mailed
options.c: 150 days from the date the notice was mailed to a U.S. address
options.d: 180 days from the date the notice was mailed

distractorExplanations.b: No 120-day rule applies; the petition is due within 90 days (150 days if addressed outside the U.S.).
distractorExplanations.c: 150 days applies when the notice is addressed to a person outside the U.S.; U.S. addresses get 90 days.
distractorExplanations.d: 180 days is not a Tax Court deadline; the deficiency petition is due 90 days after the notice is mailed.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-represent.explanation: The 90-day period is jurisdictional; missing it forecloses Tax Court review of the deficiency. Requests to pay or extensions of time to pay do not extend the period; it is 150 days if the notice is addressed outside the U.S.

options.a: Authorize a representative to receive confidential collection information from the IRS
options.b: Provide financial information for installment agreements, OIC, or CNC determinations
options.c: Request a Collection Due Process hearing after a final notice of levy
options.d: Compute the trust fund recovery penalty for responsible business officers

distractorExplanations.a: Information authorization uses Form 8821 (or 2848); Forms 433-A/B are collection financial statements.
distractorExplanations.c: CDP hearings are requested on Form 12153; Form 433-A/B supplies financial data within collection cases.
distractorExplanations.d: TFRP is proposed via Letter 1153 after a Form 4180 interview; Form 433-B describes a business's finances.

options.a: The IRS accepted a return the taxpayer filed after the extended due date
options.b: The IRS filed a return for the taxpayer that includes all available deductions
options.c: The IRS prepared a return from information documents when the taxpayer failed to file
options.d: The IRS converted a joint return to MFS after a spouse disputed it

distractorExplanations.a: A late original return filed by the taxpayer is still a taxpayer return; an SFR is prepared by the IRS for nonfilers.
distractorExplanations.b: SFRs typically use single or MFS status and the standard deduction, omitting deductions and credits the taxpayer could claim.
distractorExplanations.d: SFR has nothing to do with MFS conversions; it is an IRS-prepared basis for assessing a missing return.

options.a: Stops interest from accruing once the agreement is approved
options.b: Requires Form 433-A for every balance, even under $10,000
options.c: Reduces the balance owed to what the taxpayer can afford
options.d: Allows monthly payments when the IRS approves terms

distractorExplanations.a: Interest continues to accrue on the unpaid balance under an installment agreement; only the failure-to-pay rate drops.
distractorExplanations.b: Guaranteed and streamlined agreements under $50,000 generally need no Form 433-A financial statement.
distractorExplanations.c: Reducing the amount owed is an Offer in Compromise; an installment agreement spreads payment of the full balance.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-represent.explanation: Installment agreements accrue interest and may include user fees; larger balances may need detailed financials. Terms depend on the amount owed and the taxpayer's financial ability.

options.a: The end of the IRS period to collect assessed tax unless extended by certain events
options.b: The end of the IRS period to assess additional tax after the return is filed
options.c: The last day to claim a refund of an overpayment for the tax year
options.d: The date an installment agreement must be fully paid to avoid default

distractorExplanations.b: Assessment generally must occur within 3 years (ASED); the CSED is the 10-year collection period after assessment.
distractorExplanations.c: Refund claims follow the 3-year/2-year rule of §6511; the CSED governs IRS collection, not refunds.
distractorExplanations.d: IA terms may run to the CSED, but the CSED itself is the statutory end of the collection period.

options.a: The IRS writes off the balance after six months
options.b: The IRS pauses enforced collection
options.c: The taxpayer stops filing returns while in hardship
options.d: Penalties and interest stop accruing on the balance

distractorExplanations.a: CNC does not forgive the debt; the balance remains on the account and the CSED keeps running.
distractorExplanations.c: Taxpayers in CNC must continue filing returns; noncompliance can end CNC status.
distractorExplanations.d: Interest and the failure-to-pay penalty generally continue to accrue during CNC status.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-represent.explanation: CNC is temporary hardship relief; liabilities remain and interest may continue. CNC applies when the taxpayer cannot pay basic living expenses.

options.a: Negligent failure to deposit the employer's share of FICA
options.b: Willful failure to pay the corporation's income tax balance
options.c: Willful failure to collect or pay over withheld employment taxes
options.d: Willful failure to file Forms W-2 with the SSA on time

distractorExplanations.a: TFRP covers withheld trust fund taxes (income tax and employee FICA) and requires willfulness, not negligence.
distractorExplanations.b: Corporate income tax is not a trust fund tax; TFRP applies to withheld employment taxes.
distractorExplanations.d: Late W-2 filing triggers information-return penalties under §6721, not the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty.

options.a: Processes PTIN applications and renewals for paid return preparers
options.b: Administers the Special Enrollment Examination for EA candidates
options.c: Reviews disputed audit adjustments as an independent appeals forum
options.d: Investigates practitioner misconduct and may impose sanctions

distractorExplanations.a: PTINs are administered by the IRS Return Preparer Office; OPR handles Circular 230 discipline.
distractorExplanations.b: The SEE is run by the IRS through its testing vendor, not by OPR, whose role is disciplinary.
distractorExplanations.c: Independent review of audit disputes is the IRS Independent Office of Appeals, not OPR.

options.a: Face economic harm or have unresolved IRS problems
options.b: Want an independent review of an audit adjustment
options.c: Need free return preparation through VITA sites
options.d: Seek a private letter ruling on a proposed transaction

distractorExplanations.b: Independent review of audit adjustments is the Office of Appeals; TAS resolves hardship and systemic problems.
distractorExplanations.c: VITA and TCE provide free preparation; TAS helps with unresolved IRS problems and economic harm.
distractorExplanations.d: PLRs are issued by IRS Chief Counsel; TAS does not rule on substantive tax law questions.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-represent.explanation: TAS is an independent organization within the IRS focused on systemic and hardship cases. TAS steps in when normal IRS channels cannot fix the problem timely.

options.a: The taxpayer filed a frivolous return position
options.b: Collection of tax is in jeopardy
options.c: The assessment statute will expire within 90 days
options.d: The taxpayer has missed two installment payments

distractorExplanations.a: Frivolous returns draw the §6702 $5,000 penalty; jeopardy assessments are about collection being endangered.
distractorExplanations.c: An expiring statute calls for a statute extension or quick assessment; jeopardy depends on collection risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Missed IA payments lead to default notices and possible levy, not a jeopardy assessment.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-represent.explanation: Jeopardy assessments are extraordinary immediate assessments with limited prior notice. Typical triggers: the taxpayer may quickly leave the country or dissipate assets.

options.a: Two years from the return filing date or three years from the date the tax was paid
options.b: Three years from the date of assessment, or ten years if unpaid
options.c: Three years from the return due date (or filing date) or two years from payment
options.d: Ten years from the date of assessment, matching the CSED period

distractorExplanations.a: The periods are reversed: three years from filing or two years from payment, whichever is later.
distractorExplanations.b: The assessment date and the 10-year collection statute do not set the refund claim period under §6511.
distractorExplanations.d: Ten years is the collection statute; refund claims follow the 3-year/2-year rule of §6511.

options.a: Suspension of the taxpayer's state driver's license by the IRS
options.b: A 15% FPLP levy on Social Security benefits
options.c: Denial of a U.S. visa for the taxpayer's foreign spouse
options.d: State Department denial or revocation of a U.S. passport

distractorExplanations.a: Federal tax debt certification affects passports; driver's license suspension is a state child-support or state tax tool.
distractorExplanations.b: The Federal Payment Levy Program is a separate collection tool; §7345 certification goes to the State Department.
distractorExplanations.c: Certification affects the delinquent taxpayer's own passport, not visas for relatives.

options.a: May comply, challenge in court within time limits, or seek to quash
options.b: Must comply within 10 days or face arrest without a court order
options.c: May petition the Tax Court within 90 days to quash the summons
options.d: May ignore it unless the IRS re-serves it through state court

distractorExplanations.b: IRS summonses are enforced through a federal district court; there is no self-executing arrest power.
distractorExplanations.c: Third-party summons challenges go to federal district court (20-day petition to quash), not the Tax Court.
distractorExplanations.d: State courts play no role; IRS summonses are enforced in federal district court under §§7402 and 7604.

options.a: Extends attorney-client privilege to an accountant's return preparation work once an attorney engages the firm
options.b: May extend attorney-client privilege to an accountant hired by counsel to help the attorney provide legal advice
options.c: Gives the accountant the §7525 federally authorized practitioner privilege in criminal tax investigations
options.d: Lets the accountant represent the client before Appeals without filing a Form 2848 for the periods

distractorExplanations.a: Return preparation is not legal advice, so Kovel privilege does not cover it even when counsel hires the accountant.
distractorExplanations.c: The §7525 privilege does not apply in criminal matters, and Kovel rests on attorney-client privilege, not §7525.
distractorExplanations.d: Kovel engagements concern privilege; representation before the IRS still requires a valid Form 2848.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-represent.explanation: Kovel covers accountants engaged to assist counsel with legal advice; ordinary compliance work remains unprivileged. It does not cover routine return preparation.

options.a: Certain credits such as EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, and AOTC on paid-prepared returns
options.b: Credits such as EITC, CTC, and the Lifetime Learning Credit on any return
options.c: Credits such as the premium tax credit and dependent care credit on paid returns
options.d: The EITC only, when the client has no qualifying children

distractorExplanations.b: The Lifetime Learning Credit is not covered by Form 8867, and the form applies to paid-prepared returns.
distractorExplanations.c: Form 8867 covers EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and HOH status, not the premium tax credit or dependent care credit.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 8867 covers the EITC with or without children plus CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and HOH filing status.

options.a: E-file those returns only if clients sign Form 8948 consents
options.b: E-file those returns unless an approved hardship exception applies
options.c: E-file those returns once they file 100 or more per year
options.d: Register for an EFIN, then paper-file returns over the limit

distractorExplanations.a: Form 8948 documents a client's choice to paper file; the default for specified preparers is e-file.
distractorExplanations.c: The specified tax return preparer threshold is 11 or more individual or trust returns per year, not 100.
distractorExplanations.d: An EFIN lets a preparer e-file; it does not permit paper-filing returns that fall under the e-file mandate.

options.a: Sign the return and provide the firm's EIN instead of a PTIN
options.b: Sign the return only if they hold an EA, CPA, or attorney credential
options.c: Sign the return and provide an identification number (PTIN) on the return
options.d: Provide the PTIN but leave signing to the taxpayer alone

distractorExplanations.a: The firm EIN may also appear, but each signing preparer must enter a personal PTIN on the return.
distractorExplanations.b: Paid preparers must sign whether credentialed or not; credentials do not determine the signing duty.
distractorExplanations.d: Both the taxpayer and the paid preparer sign; the preparer's signature requirement is separate under §6695(b).

options.a: Paper-file the same return to avoid the e-file TIN match
options.b: Retransmit with the mismatched dependent removed, without asking the client first
options.c: Use an ITIN from the client's prior file to force acceptance
options.d: Contact the client, verify the correct TIN, and retransmit after correction

distractorExplanations.a: Paper filing with a wrong TIN still fails processing; the TIN must be verified and corrected first.
distractorExplanations.b: Changing a return without the client's knowledge is improper; the client must confirm data and approve changes.
distractorExplanations.c: Substituting an old ITIN without verification risks a false return; the correct current TIN must be confirmed.

options.a: Disclosure or use of tax return information without client consent or an exception
options.b: IRS employees' disclosure of return information to state tax agencies and others
options.c: Disclosure of return information by the taxpayer to a mortgage lender
options.d: Preparer advertising that guarantees refunds or IRS approval

distractorExplanations.b: IRS disclosures are governed by §6103; §7216 applies to return preparers and related persons.
distractorExplanations.c: Taxpayers may share their own information freely; §7216 restricts preparers and others in the tax business.
distractorExplanations.d: Misleading advertising falls under Circular 230 §10.30, not the §7216 return-information rules.

options.a: Is permitted if the client signs and files the return as self-prepared with no preparer
options.b: Violates preparer rules and exposes clients to errors and identity theft risk
options.c: Is permitted for preparers who file fewer than 11 returns a year
options.d: Shifts the §6694 penalties for the return onto the client

distractorExplanations.a: A client's signature does not cure the paid preparer's duty to sign and enter a PTIN under §6695.
distractorExplanations.c: Eleven returns is the e-file mandate threshold; every paid preparer must still sign and use a PTIN.
distractorExplanations.d: §6694 penalties are preparer penalties; clients face accuracy penalties for their own understatements.

options.a: More-likely-than-not support
options.b: A realistic possibility of success
options.c: Substantial authority
options.d: A supporting opinion of counsel

distractorExplanations.a: More-likely-than-not applies to tax shelters and reportable transactions; ordinary undisclosed positions need substantial authority.
distractorExplanations.b: The one-in-three realistic possibility standard was replaced in 2007; undisclosed positions now need substantial authority.
distractorExplanations.d: No opinion of counsel is required; the §6694(a) test turns on whether substantial authority supports the position.

options.a: Whether the position is likely to be audited, since low audit risk supports taking it
options.b: Whether the client is willing to pay the preparer penalty if assessed
options.c: The refund amount and whether disclosure would trigger an examination
options.d: The strength of authority supporting the position and whether disclosure is prudent

distractorExplanations.a: §10.37 and §6694 analysis may not weigh audit risk; positions are judged on their merits and authority.
distractorExplanations.b: Preparer penalties fall on the preparer and cannot be shifted by client agreement; authority strength controls.
distractorExplanations.c: Refund size and fear of examination are not proper factors; disclosure decisions turn on the level of authority.

options.a: Prompt advice to the client about the error and consequences of non-correction
options.b: Filing an amended return for the client before the statute closes
options.c: Notifying the IRS of the error if the client refuses to file an amended return
options.d: Withdrawing from all future work for the client immediately

distractorExplanations.b: Under §10.21 the practitioner advises the client; amending requires the client's decision and signature.
distractorExplanations.c: Circular 230 does not require reporting the client to the IRS; the duty is to advise and consider withdrawal.
distractorExplanations.d: Withdrawal is not required; §10.21 requires advising the client, and later conduct may affect future work.

options.a: Describe the loan as an IRS expedited refund once e-filed
options.b: Clearly disclose fees, that the loan is from a lender (not the IRS)
options.c: Disclose the loan fees only after the client signs the lender's loan documents
options.d: Present the refund transfer fee as an IRS processing charge

distractorExplanations.a: RALs are third-party loans; describing them as IRS refunds is misleading under Circular 230 §10.30.
distractorExplanations.c: Fees must be disclosed before the client commits; post-signing disclosure defeats informed consent.
distractorExplanations.d: The IRS charges no e-file processing fee; refund transfer and loan fees belong to the bank or preparer.

enrolled-agent-readiness-check-practices.explanation: Transparent RAL disclosures prevent misleading borrowers about timing and costs. Disclosures should also note that the actual refund may differ from the loan amount.

options.a: Filing Form 8821 so the IRS can lock the client's account
options.b: Filing Form 8857 to have the fraudulent return removed from the client's account
options.c: Filing Form 14039 or following IRS Identity Theft Victim Assistance procedures
options.d: Filing a paper return with a new SSN requested from the IRS

distractorExplanations.a: Form 8821 is an information authorization; identity theft victims file Form 14039 and may get an IP PIN.
distractorExplanations.b: Form 8857 requests innocent spouse relief; identity theft affidavits use Form 14039.
distractorExplanations.d: The SSA, not the IRS, issues SSNs and rarely changes them; the IRS protects victims with IP PINs.

options.a: Follow the former covered-opinion rules for any advice on listed transactions
options.b: Rely on a promoter's representations about the facts if the practitioner discloses that reliance
options.c: Include a disclaimer that the advice cannot be used to avoid penalties
options.d: Base the advice on reasonable factual and legal assumptions and consider relevant authorities

distractorExplanations.a: Covered-opinion rules (§10.35) were withdrawn in 2014; §10.37 now applies one standard to written advice.
distractorExplanations.b: Reliance on a promoter is unreasonable under §10.37 when the advisor knows or should know of the conflict.
distractorExplanations.c: The Circular 230 penalty disclaimer became unnecessary after the 2014 amendments; it is not required.

options.a: Keeping records for one year and shredding client originals after e-filing
options.b: Keeping records for the required period and returning client-owned documents on request
options.c: Keeping client originals until fees are paid and discarding workpapers after filing
options.d: Keeping only the signed Form 8879 and returning all other documents to clients

distractorExplanations.a: Preparers must keep return copies or a list for 3 years; client originals should be returned, not shredded.
distractorExplanations.c: §10.28 requires returning client records even in fee disputes, and workpapers support due diligence.
distractorExplanations.d: Form 8879 must be kept 3 years, but due diligence also requires retaining supporting records and workpapers.
